The same happens to the person: when he has resisted sins and has overcome them, then the little dogs come, against which he does not think to guard himself. These are the companions, or the society, or the trinkets, or the pastimes of men, and the kindness of men; these tear him here and there, and tug at his heart and his inner being, so that he must necessarily rot in all divine life, and in a divine earnestness, and does not feel God's grace and devotion. This small <term>temptation</term> <gloss>original: Bekörung</gloss> is often much more harmful to the person than the great <term>trials</term> <gloss>original: Anfechtungen</gloss>; for the person guards himself against these with diligence, and considers them wrong; but these small failings the person will not heed, nor consider them wrong. In the same way, just as all things that are not recognized are much more harmful than those that are recognized, so too is this danger which one does not regard or notice much, such as companionship, society, or pleasure in <term>creatures</term> <gloss>created things or worldly attachments</gloss>. Just as the deer is heated by every hunt, and its thirst increases all the more because of it, so should the person be more heated by every temptation toward divine love for our Lord. He should be provoked or driven by every trial in true thirst to run more and more into God, where he finds nothing but truth, joy, justice, and comfort. <margin>Edition of 1543.</margin>

Now the hunters sometimes do this: when the deer is too tired and exhausted, they feed the dogs a little, and these are thus held back. When they are certain of the deer in the <term>game park</term> <gloss>a fenced wooded area for hunting</gloss>, they let the deer wander about a little so that it is somewhat strengthened by it, so that it may then better endure the hunt. Our Lord does the same to the person: when He sees that the hunt is becoming too much and the trial too great, He holds it back a little. Then a drop falls into the mouth of the person's heart, which is a sweet taste of the sweetness of divine things. These strengthen him so much that all things which are not God taste bitter and <term>repulsive</term> <gloss>original: "widerzehme" or "widrig"</gloss> to him, and then it seems to him that he has completely and utterly overcome all his distress.

<summary>Tauler explains how small worldly distractions and companions can spiritually corrupt a person more than obvious sins because they go unnoticed. He uses the hunter's metaphor to describe how God provides intervals of spiritual sweetness to refresh the soul for further trials.</summary>

To summarize all that has preceded into a single concept, it is first necessary to remind the reader: that we are not discussing the origin of experience here, but rather what is contained within it. The former belongs to empirical psychology, and even there it could never be properly developed without the latter, which belongs to the critique of knowledge and particularly to the <term>understanding</term> <gloss>Verstand</gloss>.

Experience consists of <term>intuitions</term> <gloss>Anschauungen</gloss>, which belong to <term>sensibility</term> <gloss>Sinnlichkeit</gloss>, and of judgments, which are purely a task of the understanding. However, those judgments that the understanding forms solely from sensory intuitions are still far from being <term>judgments of experience</term> <gloss>Erfahrungsurtheile</gloss>. For in the one case, the judgment would only connect perceptions <note>original: "Wahrnehmungen"</note> as they are given in sensory intuition; in the latter case, however, the judgments are meant to express what experience in general contains, and thus not what is contained in mere perception, the validity of which is only subjective. The judgment of experience must therefore add something to the sensory intuition and its logical connection (after it has been made general through comparison) that defines the <term>synthetic judgment</term> <gloss>synthetische Urtheil</gloss> as necessary and thereby as universally valid. This can be nothing other than that concept which represents the intuition in relation to one form of judgment rather than another, as in itself

### CHAPTER LXVI.

**How the next day we sent messengers to the <term>Caciques</term> <gloss>local lords</gloss> of Tlaxcala, pleading with them for peace, and what they did about it.**

After the battle I have described was over, in which we captured the three principal Indians, our Captain Cortés immediately sent them out. Along with the two who were already in our camp and who had served as messengers on other occasions, he ordered them to tell the <term>Caciques</term> <gloss>local lords</gloss> of Tlaxcala that we begged them to come in peace at once, and to give us passage through their land to go to Mexico, as we have sent word to them other times. He warned that if they do not come now, we will kill all their people; and because we like them very much and wish to hold them as brothers, we would not want to anger them if they had not given cause for it. Many flattering things were said to them to draw them into our friendship. Those messengers went willingly and immediately to the capital of Tlaxcala and delivered their message to all the <term>Caciques</term> I have already named. They found them gathered with many other old men and <term>Papas</term> <gloss>indigenous priests</gloss>, and they were very sad, both because of the poor outcome of the war and the deaths of the captains, relatives, or sons of theirs who died in the battles. It is said they did not want to listen to them willingly.

What they agreed upon regarding this matter was that they immediately ordered all the diviners and <term>Papas</term>, and others who cast lots—whom they call <term>Tacalnagual</term> <gloss>sorcerers or shape-shifters</gloss>—to see through their divinations, spells, and lots what kind of people we were. They wanted to know if we could be defeated by giving us war day and night continuously, and also to know if we were <term>Teules</term> <gloss>gods or demons</gloss>, as the people of Cempoala said (who, as I have said before, are evil things like demons), and what things we ate. They were told to look into all of this with great diligence. 

<margin>What the diviners and their sorcerers said about our men.</margin> After the diviners, sorcerers, and many <term>Papas</term> gathered and performed their divinations and cast their lots and did all they were accustomed to do, it seems they said that in their lots they found that we were men of bone and flesh, and that we ate chickens, dogs, bread, and fruit when we had them, and that we did not eat the flesh of Indians or the hearts of those we killed. It appeared that the friendly Indians we brought from Cempoala had made them believe we were <term>Teules</term> and that we ate the hearts of Indians, and that the cannons threw lightning like that which falls from the sky, and that the greyhound was a tiger or lion, and that the horses were for spearing the Indians when we wanted to kill them, and they told them many other childish things. 

To return to the <term>Papas</term>: the worst thing of all that their <term>Papas</term> and diviners told them was that we could not be defeated by day, but only by night, because as night fell our strength was taken from us. <margin>The Indian diviners make them believe that we have no strength at night.</margin> Furthermore, the sorcerers told them that we were brave and that we held all these virtues during the day until the sun set, but as soon as night fell we had no strength at all. When the <term>Caciques</term> heard this and held it as very certain, they sent word to their General Captain, Xicotenga, so that he would come quickly one night with great powers to give us war. 

As soon as he knew this, he gathered about ten thousand of the bravest Indians he had and came to our camp. From three sides they began to give us a hand of arrows and throw spears with their <term>tiraderas</term> <gloss>spear-throwers</gloss> of one and two prongs, and those with swords, clubs, and two-handed swords attacked from another side. Once the sick had recovered, and since we had been there for three days, the women we had sent out arrived. They reported that they had found very few people, as most had gone to hunt the <term>vacas</term> <gloss>cows, referring to the American bison</gloss>, as it was the season for it. We ordered those who had been sick to stay behind and those who were healthy to go with us. We planned that two days' journey from there, those same women would go with two of our men to bring people out to the road to receive us. With this arrangement, the next morning all those who were strongest departed with us. After three days of travel, we halted, and the following day Alonso del Castillo set out with <term>Estebanico</term> <gloss>an enslaved North African man and one of the four survivors</gloss> the Black man, taking the two women as guides.

The woman who was a captive led them to a river that ran between some mountain ranges where there was a town in which her father lived. These were the first houses we saw that had the appearance and structure of permanent dwellings. Here, Castillo and Estebanico reached the place where we had stayed and brought back five or six of those Indians. He told us how he had found houses of settled people who ate <term>frisoles</term> <gloss>beans</gloss> and <term>calabazas</term> <gloss>squash or gourds</gloss>, and that he had seen <term>maiz</term> <gloss>maize or corn</gloss>. This was the thing in the world that gladdened us most, and for it we gave infinite thanks to our Lord. Castillo said that the Black man was coming with all the people from the houses to wait on the road nearby. 

For this reason we departed, and after walking a league and a half, we met the Black man and the people coming to receive us. They gave us beans and many squash to eat, as well as gourds to carry water, robes made of bison hide, and other things. As these people and those who came with us were enemies and did not understand each other, we took leave of the first group, giving them what had been given to us, and went with these new people. Six leagues from there, as night was falling, we reached their houses, where they held great festivities for us. We stayed here one day, and the next we departed, taking them with us to other settled houses where the people ate the same things.

From then on, there was a new custom: those who knew of our coming did not come out to receive us on the roads as the others had done. Instead, we found them in their houses, and they had built other houses for us. They were all seated, with their faces turned toward the wall, their heads bowed, and their hair pulled over their eyes. Their belongings were placed in a pile in the middle of the house. From this point forward, they began to give us many robes made of skins, and there was nothing they possessed that they did not give to us. These are the people of the finest bodies we saw, possessing great vitality and ability, and they understood us and responded to our questions better than any others. We called them the People of the Cows, because most of the bison are killed near there, and for more than fifty leagues up that river, the people go out to kill many of them. 

These people go entirely naked, in the manner of the first ones we found. The women go covered with deer skins, as do a few men, specifically the old ones who are no longer fit for war. It is a very well populated land. We asked them why they did not sow maize; they replied that they did so to avoid losing what they planted, because for two years in a row the rains had failed. The weather had been so dry that the moles had destroyed all their maize, and they would not dare to plant again until it had first rained heavily. They begged us to tell the sky to rain and to pray for it, and we promised them we would do so. 

We also wanted to know where they had brought that maize from, and they told us it came from where the sun sets, and that it existed throughout all that land, but that the nearest source was along that path. We asked them which way we should go, and for information about the road, because they did not want to go there. They told us the path was up that river toward the North, and that in seventeen days of travel we would find nothing else to eat but a fruit they call <term>chacán</term> <gloss>likely the fruit of the yucca or a similar desert plant</gloss>. They mash it between stones, but even after this effort, it is difficult to eat because it is so harsh and dry. This was the truth, for they showed it to us there and we could not eat it. They also told us that while we traveled up the river, we would always be among people who were their enemies but spoke the same language. Those people would have no food to give us, but they would receive us with very good will and give us many cotton blankets, skins, and other things they possessed. Still, they felt that we should by no means take that path.

Doubting what we should do and which path would better suit our purpose and benefit, we stayed with them for two days. They gave us beans and squash to eat. Their method of cooking them is so new that, because it is so, I wanted to include it here, so that it may be seen and known how diverse and strange the ingenuity and industry of human men are. They do not possess pots. To cook what they wish, they fill half of a large gourd with water. In the fire, they throw many stones of the kind that are most easily heated. When they see the stones are glowing, they take them with wooden tongs and throw them into the water in the gourd until they make it boil with the heat the stones carry. When they see the water is boiling, they throw in what they are to cook. Throughout this time, they do nothing but take out some stones and throw in other glowing ones so that the water keeps boiling to cook what they want, and thus they cook it.
